facts: Albania was the most isolated country in Europe under Enver Hoxha, who had several hundred thousand concrete bunkers built across the countryside; many still sit in fields and on beaches today.
Private cars were banned for ordinary citizens until 1991, so the country went from almost no traffic to full motorisation within a single generation.
The Albanian language forms its own independent branch of the Indo-European family, with no close living relatives.
AL.about: Mountains cover most of Albania, rising from a narrow coastal plain on the Adriatic and Ionian seas to the limestone ranges of the Albanian Alps in the north and the high ground along the eastern frontier. Large lakes are shared with neighbours at Shkodër, Ohrid and Prespa, while the Vjosa, which runs largely undammed from the Pindus to the sea, is often described as one of Europe's last wild rivers. For more than four centuries the region was part of the Ottoman Empire, and the national hero Skanderbeg is remembered for leading resistance to the Ottomans in the 15th century. Independence was proclaimed at Vlorë in November 1912. After communism collapsed in the early 1990s, large numbers of Albanians emigrated to Italy, Greece and beyond, and money sent home remains important. Tourism along the southern coastline, the so-called Albanian Riviera, has grown rapidly in recent years.

facts: Andorra has two heads of state at once: the President of France and the Bishop of Urgell in Spain, an arrangement dating from 1278.
At 1,023 metres, Andorra la Vella is the highest capital city in Europe.
The country has no airport and no railway; every visitor arrives by road through the Pyrenees.
AD.about: Squeezed into the eastern Pyrenees, Andorra consists almost entirely of steep mountains and the deep glacial valleys of the Valira river and its branches, where nearly all settlement and roads are concentrated. Winters are snowy and summers mild, which has made skiing the backbone of the economy alongside shopping, as low taxes have long drawn visitors from France and Spain to buy goods more cheaply. The principality is one of the last survivors of the small medieval states of the Pyrenees, but its modern political form is recent: a written constitution was adopted by referendum in 1993, establishing a parliamentary democracy, and Andorra joined the United Nations the same year. It is not a member of the European Union, though it has an agreement allowing it to issue euro coins. Andorran citizens are a minority of residents; many inhabitants are Spanish, Portuguese or French nationals who came to work in tourism and services.

facts: Austria borders eight countries, more than any other European state except Germany, Russia and Serbia.
Around 62% of the country lies within the Alps, which is why its population concentrates along the Danube in the flatter east.
Vienna draws most of its drinking water directly from Alpine springs through pipelines built in the 1870s.
AT.about: The Danube crosses northern Austria from west to east, passing Linz and the vineyards of the Wachau valley before reaching Vienna, and the plains near the Hungarian border hold Lake Neusiedl, a shallow steppe lake ringed by reeds. For more than six centuries this was the heartland of the Habsburg dynasty, whose empire stretched across much of Central Europe until its collapse at the end of the First World War in 1918 left a small German-speaking republic. Austria was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938 and, after 1945, occupied by the four Allied powers for a decade. The State Treaty of 1955 restored full sovereignty, and the country declared permanent neutrality the same year. It joined the European Union in 1995. Today Vienna is one of the seats of the United Nations, and the economy combines advanced manufacturing with year-round tourism built on skiing, lakes and the musical heritage of composers such as Mozart and Haydn.

facts: Belarus is one of the flattest countries in Europe; its highest point is a hill barely taller than a 100-storey building.
Around a fifth of the country is forest and marshland, including Belovezhskaya Pushcha, one of the last primeval forests on the continent.
It is among the few European countries that never had a coastline at any point in its history.
BY.about: Glacial plains and low moraine ridges define Belarus, with the Braslaw lake district and Lake Narach in the north and the vast wetlands of Polesia along the Pripyat river in the south. The Dnieper and Neman rivers carry water towards the Black Sea and the Baltic respectively. For centuries these lands belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and then the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, before passing to the Russian Empire in the partitions of the late 18th century. As a Soviet republic, Belarus suffered enormous losses in the Second World War, when hundreds of villages were destroyed, and in 1986 much of the south-east was contaminated by fallout from the Chernobyl disaster just across the border. It became independent when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991 and has since kept close political and economic ties with Russia. Much of the economy remains state-run, with heavy trucks, tractors and potash fertiliser among its best-known exports.

facts: Belgium has three official languages — Dutch, French and German — and a federal structure built around that divide.
Brussels hosts the headquarters of both the European Union and NATO.
The port of Antwerp is one of the largest in Europe and handles a substantial share of the continent's chemical trade.
BE.about: From a short, sandy North Sea coast lined with dunes and resorts, Belgium rises gently through the fertile plains of Flanders and the central plateau to the wooded hills of the Ardennes in the south-east. Two major rivers, the Scheldt and the Meuse, made the area a crossroads of trade long before the state existed. Belgium broke away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in a revolution in 1830 and became a constitutional monarchy the following year. It was among the first places in continental Europe to industrialise, with coal mining and steelmaking concentrated in Wallonia, but the decline of heavy industry in the 20th century shifted economic weight north to Flanders. The country's position between larger powers made it a battleground in both world wars, and the fields around Ypres remain a focus of remembrance. Today it is densely populated, highly urbanised and closely tied to the institutions of European integration.

facts: Bosnia and Herzegovina has roughly 20 kilometres of coastline at Neum, which splits Croatia's territory in two.
The country has a three-member presidency, with one Bosniak, one Croat and one Serb member serving at the same time.
The 1984 Winter Olympics were held in Sarajevo; several of the venues were damaged during the siege of the city a decade later.
BA.about: Most of Bosnia and Herzegovina is taken up by the Dinaric Alps, a rugged belt of limestone mountains, karst plateaus and deep river gorges. The Sava marks much of the northern border, the Drina much of the eastern one, and the emerald Neretva cuts south through Mostar towards the Adriatic. Bosnia in the north has a continental climate, while Herzegovina in the south is warmer and drier. The Ottomans conquered the region in the 15th century, leaving a lasting legacy of mosques, bridges and a large Muslim community. Austria-Hungary took control in 1878, and the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered the First World War. After decades within Yugoslavia, the country declared independence in 1992, followed by a devastating war that ended with the Dayton Agreement in 1995. That settlement divided the state into two entities, the Federation and Republika Srpska, plus the separately governed Brčko District.

facts: Musala is the highest peak in the whole Balkan Peninsula, not just in Bulgaria.
Plovdiv is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, with settlement traces going back some 8,000 years.
Bulgaria produces a large share of the world's rose oil, distilled in the Valley of the Roses near Kazanlak.
BG.about: Bulgaria is divided almost in two by the Balkan Mountains, which run east to west across its centre; to the north lies the Danube plain, much of it along the Romanian border, and to the south the warm Thracian lowlands, with the Rila and Pirin ranges rising in the south-west and a Black Sea coast in the east. A Bulgarian state was first established in 681, and during the First Bulgarian Empire scholars developed the Cyrillic alphabet, which spread to Russia, Serbia and many other lands. From the late 14th century the country spent nearly five hundred years under Ottoman rule, regaining autonomy in 1878 after a Russo-Turkish war and full independence in 1908. Communist government lasted from the 1940s until 1989. Bulgaria joined the European Union in 2007. Since 1990 its population has fallen sharply because of emigration and low birth rates, a trend especially visible in rural villages.

facts: Croatia's coastline includes more than 1,200 islands, though fewer than 50 are permanently inhabited.
The country is shaped like a crescent, and its territory is interrupted near Neum by Bosnia and Herzegovina's short coastal strip.
The necktie descends from the scarves worn by Croatian mercenaries in 17th-century France — 'cravate' comes from 'Croat'.
HR.about: Two very different landscapes meet in Croatia: the flat, fertile Pannonian lowlands of Slavonia between the Drava and Sava rivers in the north-east, and the long limestone coastline of Istria and Dalmatia on the Adriatic, separated by the bare karst ranges of the Dinaric Alps. Inland, the Plitvice Lakes form a chain of terraced turquoise pools linked by waterfalls. Croatia entered a union with the Hungarian crown in 1102 and later came under Habsburg rule, while the city-republic of Dubrovnik, known as Ragusa, remained an independent maritime power for centuries. After 1918 the country became part of Yugoslavia. It declared independence in June 1991, which was followed by war until 1995. Croatia joined the European Union in 2013 and the Schengen area in 2023. Tourism is now one of the largest parts of the economy, and summer visitors greatly outnumber residents in many coastal towns.

facts: Czechia has the highest beer consumption per person of any country in the world.
Charles University in Prague, founded in 1348, is the oldest university in Central Europe.
The country split peacefully from Slovakia on 1 January 1993 in what is usually called the Velvet Divorce.
CZ.about: Made up of the historic lands of Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia, Czechia sits on a major European watershed: the Vltava and Elbe drain towards the North Sea, the Morava flows to the Danube and the Black Sea, and the Oder heads for the Baltic. Bohemia is a broad basin almost enclosed by forested mountains, including the Krkonoše, the Šumava and the Ore Mountains, while Moravia to the east is lower and known for its vineyards. Bohemia was a powerful kingdom in the Middle Ages and later part of the Habsburg monarchy for about four centuries. Czechoslovakia was founded on 28 October 1918, dismembered after the Munich Agreement of 1938, and came under communist rule in 1948; the Prague Spring reforms were crushed in 1968, and the Velvet Revolution ended communism in 1989. Today Czechia is one of Europe's most industrialised countries, with car manufacturing, led by Škoda, at the heart of its economy.

facts: Denmark proper consists of the Jutland peninsula and around 400 islands, roughly 70 of which are inhabited.
Its highest natural point is lower than many office buildings, making it one of the flattest countries in Europe.
The Kingdom of Denmark also includes Greenland and the Faroe Islands, both self-governing.
DK.about: Shaped by ice-age glaciers that left low hills, moraines and fertile clay soils, Denmark is a country of farmland, beech woods and long coastlines; no one lives more than about 50 kilometres from the sea. The west coast of Jutland faces the North Sea with dunes and the tidal flats of the Wadden Sea, while the islands to the east are linked by major bridges, including the Øresund Bridge to Sweden, opened in 2000. Danish Vikings raided and settled widely, and the monarchy is one of the oldest in the world. In the late Middle Ages Denmark led the Kalmar Union of the Nordic kingdoms, but it later lost Norway in 1814 and Schleswig-Holstein to Prussia in 1864. A constitution in 1849 made it a constitutional monarchy. Today Denmark is a leader in wind energy, which supplies around half of its electricity, and it exports large quantities of pork and dairy products.

facts: Estonia was the first country to hold legally binding general elections over the internet, in 2005.
More than half the country is covered by forest, and it has over 2,000 islands in the Baltic Sea.
Estonian is closely related to Finnish and unrelated to the Indo-European languages spoken by most of its neighbours.
EE.about: Low and gently rolling, Estonia was scraped flat by glaciers and is dotted with bogs, lakes and limestone; along the Gulf of Finland the land ends abruptly at the North Estonian Klint, a line of cliffs in places over 50 metres high. Lake Peipus, one of Europe's largest lakes, forms much of the eastern border. For centuries the territory was ruled in turn by Danish kings, the Teutonic Order, Sweden and, from the early 18th century, the Russian Empire, with a Baltic German nobility dominating land and towns. Estonia declared independence in February 1918, was occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940 and regained independence in August 1991 after the peaceful Singing Revolution. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004. The north-east, around Narva, has a large Russian-speaking population and is the centre of oil shale mining, while Tallinn has built a reputation as a hub for software start-ups.

facts: Finland has roughly 188,000 lakes, more relative to its size than any other country.
About a quarter of its territory lies north of the Arctic Circle, where the sun does not set for weeks in summer.
Finnish belongs to the Uralic family alongside Estonian and Hungarian, not to the Indo-European family.
FI.about: Finland was shaped by the last ice age, which left ridges of gravel, granite outcrops and countless lake basins; the land is still slowly rising as it recovers from the weight of the ice, most noticeably along the Gulf of Bothnia. Forests cover around three quarters of the country, which has long supported a large timber, pulp and paper industry. Most people live in the milder south, especially around Helsinki. For roughly six centuries Finland was part of the Swedish realm, and in 1809 it became an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire. It declared independence on 6 December 1917, survived a brief civil war in 1918, and lost parts of Karelia to the Soviet Union after the Winter War of 1939 to 1940. Swedish remains an official language, and the Åland Islands are autonomous and Swedish-speaking. Finland joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2023.

facts: Counting its overseas departments, France spans twelve time zones — more than any other country.
It is the most visited country in the world by international arrivals.
Because of French Guiana in South America, France's longest land border is with Brazil.
FR.about: Roughly hexagonal in shape, France faces three seas — the English Channel, the Atlantic and the Mediterranean — and is framed by mountains: the Pyrenees, the Alps and the Jura, with the volcanic uplands of the Massif Central at its heart and the island of Corsica offshore. Four great river systems, the Seine, Loire, Garonne and Rhône, drain fertile basins that have made France the largest agricultural producer in the European Union, famous for wine, cheese and grain. The Revolution of 1789 overthrew the monarchy and spread ideas of citizenship and secular government across Europe. The present constitution dates from 1958, when the Fifth Republic was established, and France was a founding member of the communities that became the European Union. Government, business and culture are unusually centralised in Paris, whose region holds nearly a fifth of the population. Nuclear power generates the majority of the country's electricity.

facts: Germany borders nine countries, more than any other in Europe apart from Russia.
It was unified as a single nation state only in 1871, and divided again from 1949 until 1990.
Roughly a third of the country is forested, and it has more than 20,000 castles and fortified houses.
DE.about: From the sandy coasts of the North Sea and Baltic, Germany rises through the broad North German Plain to the forested central uplands, such as the Harz and Black Forest, and finally to a narrow strip of the Alps along the Bavarian border. The Rhine, Elbe and Danube, which begins in the Black Forest, have carried trade for centuries. For most of its history the region was a patchwork of kingdoms, duchies and free cities within the Holy Roman Empire, and that legacy survives in today's federal system of 16 states, each with its own government. Unlike many European countries, Germany has no single dominant city; economic life is spread between Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Frankfurt and the old industrial Ruhr. It has the largest economy in Europe, built on exports of cars, machinery and chemicals, and it completed its phase-out of nuclear power in 2023 while expanding wind and solar energy.

facts: Greece has around 6,000 islands and islets, of which roughly 227 are inhabited.
No part of the country is more than about 137 kilometres from the sea.
Its merchant fleet is among the largest in the world by tonnage, despite the country's small population.
GR.about: Around four fifths of Greece is mountainous, with the Pindus range running down the mainland like a spine, and fertile land is limited to coastal plains and valleys such as those of Thessaly and Macedonia. Summers are hot and dry, winters mild on the coast, ideal for olives, grapes and citrus. The Peloponnese peninsula is separated from the rest of the mainland by the Corinth Canal, opened in 1893. Ancient Greece gave Europe early forms of democracy, philosophy and theatre, but the modern state emerged only after the War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire began in 1821, with independence recognised in 1830. Its borders expanded in stages, notably after the Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913 and with the Dodecanese islands in 1947. A military junta ruled from 1967 to 1974, after which the monarchy was abolished by referendum. Greece joined the European Community in 1981, and tourism and shipping dominate the economy.

facts: Lake Balaton is the largest lake in Central Europe and is sometimes called the Hungarian Sea.
Budapest was formed in 1873 by merging Buda and Óbuda on one bank of the Danube with Pest on the other.
Hungarian is a Uralic language, unrelated to the Slavic and Germanic tongues surrounding it.
HU.about: Lying in the centre of the Carpathian Basin, Hungary is mostly lowland: east of the Danube stretches the Great Hungarian Plain, a flat expanse of farmland and grassy puszta crossed by the Tisza river, while Transdanubia to the west is hillier. The country sits on top of abundant geothermal water, and Hungary is known for its thermal baths, including the warm lake at Hévíz. The Magyars arrived in the basin around 895, and Stephen I was crowned the first king around 1000. After defeat by the Ottomans at Mohács in 1526 the kingdom was partitioned, then came under the Habsburgs, and from 1867 it formed half of the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary. The Treaty of Trianon in 1920 cost Hungary about two thirds of its former territory, leaving large Hungarian-speaking communities in neighbouring states. The 1956 uprising against Soviet control was suppressed, but the country left communism behind in 1989 and joined the European Union in 2004.

facts: Iceland sits astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, so the island is slowly being pulled apart between two tectonic plates.
Almost all of its electricity and heating comes from hydro and geothermal sources.
The Althing, founded around 930, is often described as the oldest surviving parliament in the world.
IS.about: Glaciers, lava fields and volcanoes dominate Iceland, whose largely uninhabited interior is a high plateau of rock and ice; Vatnajökull in the south-east is one of the largest ice caps in Europe. Thanks to the North Atlantic Current, the coasts are far milder than the island's latitude just south of the Arctic Circle would suggest. Norse settlers, traditionally dated to 874, arrived from Scandinavia with Gaelic companions and recorded their history in the medieval sagas. Iceland came under the Norwegian crown in the 13th century and later under Denmark, becoming a sovereign kingdom in union with Denmark in 1918 and a fully independent republic in 1944. About two thirds of the population lives in and around the capital. Fishing long sustained the economy and led to the Cod Wars with Britain; aluminium smelting, powered by cheap energy, and tourism are now equally important. The 2010 eruption of Eyjafjallajökull disrupted air travel across Europe.

facts: Ireland has no native snakes, a fact folklore credits to Saint Patrick but which glaciation explains better.
The Great Famine of the 1840s cut the population by around a quarter through death and emigration, and it has still not returned to its pre-famine peak.
Its only land border is with Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom.
IE.about: Ireland is often compared to a saucer: a low central plain of farmland, lakes and peat bog is ringed by coastal hills and mountains, many of them in the rugged west and south-west. The River Shannon, the longest in the British Isles, flows through the middle of the island. Mild, wet weather from the Atlantic keeps the countryside green and makes pasture farming dominant. Ireland was governed from Britain for centuries and formed part of the United Kingdom from 1801. The Easter Rising of 1916 and the War of Independence led to the Anglo-Irish Treaty and the creation of the Irish Free State in 1922, while the six counties of Northern Ireland remained in the UK; the state formally became a republic in 1949. Irish is the first official language, spoken daily mainly in western Gaeltacht areas. After joining the European Community in 1973, Ireland attracted many multinational technology and pharmaceutical firms, transforming its economy.

facts: Italy completely surrounds two other sovereign states, San Marino and Vatican City.
It has more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country.
Mount Etna in Sicily is the most active volcano in Europe and has been erupting on and off for at least 2,700 years.
IT.about: A long peninsula reaching into the Mediterranean, Italy is framed by the Alps in the north and traversed by the Apennines, which run almost its entire length. Between the two lies the Po Valley, the country's largest plain and the core of its farming and industry, while Sicily and Sardinia are the two largest islands in the Mediterranean. Earthquakes and volcanoes, including Vesuvius near Naples, reflect the region's restless geology. After the fall of Rome the peninsula remained divided among city-states, kingdoms and foreign powers for some fourteen centuries, until the Risorgimento brought unification as a kingdom in 1861; Rome became the capital in 1871. Italy voted to become a republic in 1946 and was a founding member of the European Economic Community, created by the Treaty of Rome in 1957. A persistent economic gap separates the industrial north from the poorer south, and the population is among the oldest in Europe.

facts: Riga has one of the largest collections of Art Nouveau architecture of any city in the world.
Latvia is about half forest, one of the highest proportions in the European Union.
The Baltic Way of 1989 saw two million people form a human chain across Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia.
LV.about: Latvia is a low country of farmland, forest, bogs and glacial lakes, with a long sandy coastline on the Baltic Sea and the Gulf of Riga. The Daugava, its principal river, flows across the country from Belarus to the sea at Riga, and was for centuries a trade route between the Baltic and Russia. Riga was founded in 1201 by German crusaders and became a prosperous Hanseatic port, and Baltic German landowners remained powerful under later Polish, Swedish and Russian rule. Latvia declared independence on 18 November 1918, was occupied by the Soviet Union in 1940 and regained independence in 1991. Large-scale Soviet-era migration left a sizeable Russian-speaking minority, concentrated in Riga and in eastern Latgale. Around a third of Latvians live in the capital. The country joined the European Union and NATO in 2004, and its Song and Dance Festival, held every few years with tens of thousands of performers, is a central part of national identity.

facts: Liechtenstein is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, meaning every neighbour is landlocked too.
It has no airport and no army, having disbanded its forces in 1868.
The country produces more registered companies than it has residents.
LI.about: Wedged between the Alps and the Rhine, Liechtenstein has two distinct parts: a flat strip along the river, which forms the border with Switzerland and holds most of the towns, farms and factories, and a mountainous east of high valleys and peaks. The principality was created in 1719, when the Holy Roman Emperor combined the lordships of Vaduz and Schellenberg under the Liechtenstein family, and it became sovereign in 1806. The princes lived mainly in Vienna until 1938. Since 1923 the country has had a customs union with Switzerland, and it is a member of the European Economic Area and the Schengen area, though not of the European Union. Its constitutional monarchy gives the prince unusually strong powers by European standards. Despite its size, Liechtenstein is highly industrialised, with companies making precision tools and dental products, and more than half of its workforce commutes in from Switzerland and Austria.

facts: Lithuania was the first Soviet republic to declare independence, in March 1990.
The medieval Grand Duchy of Lithuania was at one point the largest state in Europe.
Its border with Russia is with Kaliningrad, an exclave separated from the rest of the country.
LT.about: The largest of the three Baltic states, Lithuania is a gently rolling landscape of glacial hills, lakes and farmland drained mainly by the Nemunas river. Its short coastline includes part of the Curonian Spit, a narrow ribbon of high sand dunes shared with Russia and listed by UNESCO, and the Baltic shore has long been known for amber. Lithuania was the last pagan state in Europe, formally adopting Christianity in 1387 after its grand duke became King of Poland. The two states merged into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1569, which was partitioned in the late 18th century, leaving most of Lithuania under Russian rule. Independence was declared on 16 February 1918, though Vilnius was held by Poland between the wars and Kaunas served as the temporary capital. Lithuanian, a Baltic language, preserves many archaic Indo-European features. The country joined the European Union and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2015.

facts: Luxembourg is the world's only remaining sovereign grand duchy, a title that once applied to several European states.
It has among the highest GDP per capita of any country, driven largely by banking and investment funds.
In 2020 it became the first country to make all public transport free nationwide.
LU.about: Two quite different landscapes divide this small state. The northern third, the Oesling, belongs to the Ardennes plateau: wooded uplands cut by deep, winding river valleys. The southern Gutland, or “good land”, is gentler farming country, edged in the east by the vineyards of the Moselle valley along the German border. In the far south, iron ore deposits fed a steel industry that made the country wealthy long before finance took over. The Congress of Vienna created the grand duchy in 1815 under the Dutch king; it lost its western, French-speaking half to Belgium in 1839, was declared neutral in 1867 and gained its own dynasty in 1890. Occupied by Germany in both world wars, it later became a founding member of NATO and the European communities, and hosts the EU’s Court of Justice. Nearly half of residents are foreign nationals, and everyday life moves easily between Luxembourgish, French and German.

facts: Malta is one of the most densely populated countries in the world, with the whole nation smaller than many cities.
Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet and the only one that is an official EU language.
The Ġgantija temples on Gozo predate both Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids.
MT.about: Lying in the central Mediterranean roughly 90 kilometres south of Sicily, the Maltese archipelago consists of three inhabited islands, Malta, Gozo and tiny Comino, built largely of soft golden limestone. There are no permanent rivers, rainfall is concentrated in the mild winters, and much of the drinking water now comes from desalination. Its harbours made it a prize for every Mediterranean power: Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs, Normans and, from 1530, the Knights of St John, who withstood the Ottoman Great Siege of 1565 and then built Valletta as a fortified city. Britain took control in the early 1800s and used the islands as a naval base; their endurance under bombing in the Second World War earned Malta the George Cross in 1942. Independence followed in 1964 and the country became a republic in 1974, joining the EU in 2004. Tourism, financial services, online gaming and one of the world’s largest ship registers now drive the economy.

facts: Moldova's Cricova and Mileștii Mici cellars hold some of the largest wine collections in the world, stored in tunnels tens of kilometres long.
The country is landlocked apart from a few hundred metres of Danube frontage at Giurgiulești, which gives it a river port.
Transnistria, a strip east of the Dniester, has operated outside government control since 1992.
MD.about: Squeezed between the Prut river in the west and the Dniester in the east, Moldova is a country of rolling hills and deep black soils, ideal for vineyards, orchards and sunflowers. The wooded Codri uplands occupy the centre, while the south opens into drier steppe. Most of the territory corresponds to Bessarabia, the eastern half of the medieval principality of Moldavia, which the Russian Empire annexed in 1812. It joined Romania in 1918, was taken by the Soviet Union in 1940 and became the Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic. Independence came in August 1991, shortly after the language had returned to the Latin alphabet. In the south, the autonomous region of Gagauzia is home to a Turkic-speaking Orthodox Christian people. Moldova remains one of Europe’s poorer countries, heavily reliant on agriculture and on money sent home by workers abroad, and it was granted EU candidate status in 2022.

facts: Monaco is the second smallest country in the world and the most densely populated.
It has expanded its territory by around 20% since the 1960s by reclaiming land from the sea.
The Monaco Grand Prix is run on public streets that are returned to normal traffic within days.
MC.about: Monaco occupies a narrow strip of Riviera coastline where the Maritime Alps drop steeply into the Mediterranean, close to the Italian border. There is no countryside at all: the whole state is urban, arranged in terraces climbing the hillside, with the old town and Prince’s Palace perched on the Rock, a rocky headland overlooking the harbour. The Grimaldi family seized the Rock in 1297 and has ruled, with interruptions, ever since. In 1861 Monaco gave up the towns of Menton and Roquebrune to France in exchange for recognition of its independence, and Prince Charles III turned to tourism, opening the casino and lending his name to Monte Carlo. The abolition of personal income tax in 1869 helped make the principality a magnet for wealthy residents, and Monégasque citizens are now a minority in their own country. France is responsible for its defence, and it joined the United Nations in 1993.

facts: Montenegro restored its independence in 2006 after a referendum ended its union with Serbia.
The Bay of Kotor is a deeply indented inlet often described, inaccurately but persistently, as Europe's southernmost fjord.
The country uses the euro despite never having been a member of the European Union.
ME.about: Its name, “Black Mountain”, recalls the dark forested slopes of the Dinaric Alps that cover most of the country. Behind a short Adriatic coast of old walled towns, the land rises abruptly into bare limestone karst and then into high massifs such as Durmitor, where the Tara River has carved one of the deepest canyons in Europe. Lake Skadar, shared with Albania, is the largest lake in the Balkans and an important refuge for birds. The rugged interior helped Montenegrins resist full Ottoman control; from the late 17th century they were led by prince-bishops of the Petrović-Njegoš family, ruling from the old royal capital of Cetinje. The Congress of Berlin recognised Montenegro’s independence in 1878, and it became a kingdom in 1910 before joining what became Yugoslavia in 1918. A member of NATO since 2017 and a candidate for EU membership, it relies heavily on summer tourism along the coast.

facts: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level, protected by an extensive system of dikes and pumps.
Amsterdam is the constitutional capital, but the government, parliament and royal residence are in The Hague.
The country is one of the world's largest agricultural exporters despite its small size, largely through greenhouse horticulture.
NL.about: Much of the country is a delta, built up where the Rhine, Meuse and Scheldt reach the North Sea, and much of it has been shaped by people as much as by nature. Over centuries the Dutch drained lakes and marshes into polders; in the 20th century the Afsluitdijk dam closed off the Zuiderzee, turning it into the freshwater IJsselmeer and making room for Flevoland, a province created entirely from reclaimed land. After the North Sea flood of 1953, the Delta Works sealed the south-western estuaries. The Dutch Republic emerged from a revolt against Spanish rule that began in 1568 and was recognised in 1648, and in the 17th century its trading companies made it a leading commercial power. A kingdom since 1815, it now has its population concentrated in the Randstad, the ring of cities in the west, while Rotterdam is Europe’s busiest port. Cycling is part of daily life.

facts: The country added 'North' to its name in 2019 to settle a long dispute with Greece over the name Macedonia.
Lake Ohrid, shared with Albania, is among the oldest and deepest lakes in Europe.
It is landlocked and mountainous, with more than fifty peaks above 2,000 metres.
MK.about: The Vardar river is the backbone of the country, flowing from the north-west past Skopje and out through a gorge into Greece, where it reaches the Aegean as the Axios. Its valley channels warm Mediterranean air northward, and the hot, dry summers of the Tikveš area support a long tradition of winemaking, while the surrounding uplands have a harsher continental climate. For roughly five centuries the region was part of the Ottoman Empire, until the Balkan Wars of 1912–13 divided historic Macedonia between Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria. After the Second World War it became a republic within Yugoslavia, and it declared independence peacefully in 1991. A devastating earthquake in 1963 destroyed much of Skopje, which was rebuilt largely to modern plans. Ethnic Albanians make up roughly a quarter of the population, and the 2001 Ohrid Agreement expanded their rights after a short conflict. The country joined NATO in 2020.

facts: Norway's coastline, counting fjords and islands, runs to well over 100,000 kilometres.
Its sovereign wealth fund, built on North Sea oil, is the largest in the world.
Svalbard, far to the north, is Norwegian territory but open to citizens of all treaty signatories to live and work.
NO.about: Stretching along the western edge of the Scandinavian Peninsula, Norway is long, narrow and mountainous, with only a small share of its land suitable for farming. Ice-age glaciers gouged the deep valleys that the sea later flooded, and inland lie broad high plateaus such as Hardangervidda. Much of the north lies above the Arctic Circle, with midnight sun in summer and polar night in winter, yet the warm North Atlantic Current keeps most of the coast free of ice. After centuries in union with Denmark, Norway adopted its own constitution at Eidsvoll on 17 May 1814, now the national day, but was then joined to Sweden under a shared king until a peaceful separation in 1905. Hydropower supplies almost all of its electricity. Voters twice rejected joining the European Union, in 1972 and 1994, although Norway takes part in the single market through the EEA. The Sámi are the indigenous people of the far north.

facts: Poland disappeared from the map entirely between 1795 and 1918, partitioned between three empires.
Białowieża Forest on the Belarusian border is one of the last remaining fragments of Europe's primeval lowland forest.
Warsaw's old town was rebuilt almost from scratch after 1945, using paintings as reference, and is now a World Heritage Site.
PL.about: The name is often traced to the Polanie, “people of the fields”, and most of Poland is indeed part of the great North European Plain. The Vistula, its longest river, runs from the Carpathians past Kraków and Warsaw to the Baltic near Gdańsk, while the Oder marks much of the western border. The north has a sandy Baltic coast and the Masurian Lake District, with thousands of glacial lakes; the south rises into the Sudetes and the Tatra Mountains. The baptism of Duke Mieszko I in 966 is traditionally taken as the birth of the state, and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth later became one of Europe’s largest powers. After the Second World War, the country’s borders were shifted far westward. The Solidarity trade union movement, founded in 1980, helped bring an end to communist rule in 1989. Poland joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004, and has since been one of the region’s fastest-growing economies.

facts: Portugal's mainland border with Spain is one of the oldest continuously settled borders in Europe, largely fixed since 1297.
The country produces about half the world's cork, harvested from oak bark without felling the trees.
Its highest point is not on the mainland but on Pico Island in the Azores, over 1,500 kilometres out in the Atlantic.
PT.about: Occupying the western strip of the Iberian Peninsula, Portugal faces the Atlantic along its whole coast, and Cabo da Roca near Lisbon is the westernmost point of mainland Europe. The Tagus roughly divides a greener, more mountainous north, where terraced vineyards line the Douro valley, from the flatter, hotter Alentejo and the sunny Algarve coast in the south. The Atlantic archipelagos of Madeira and the Azores are autonomous regions. Portugal became a kingdom in the 12th century under Afonso Henriques and, from the 15th century, its navigators led Europe’s maritime expansion: Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498 and Brazil was claimed in 1500. A huge earthquake devastated Lisbon in 1755. The monarchy fell in 1910, and decades of dictatorship ended with the largely bloodless Carnation Revolution of 1974, after which the African colonies gained independence. Portugal joined the European Community in 1986, and tourism is now a major industry.

facts: The Danube Delta, where the river meets the Black Sea, is the best-preserved river delta in Europe.
Romanian is a Romance language, descended from Latin, surrounded on almost all sides by Slavic and Hungarian speakers.
The Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest is among the heaviest buildings ever constructed.
RO.about: The arc of the Carpathian Mountains curves through the middle of Romania, enclosing the Transylvanian plateau; outside the arc lie the broad plains of Wallachia to the south and Moldavia to the east. The Danube forms much of the southern border, cutting through the dramatic Iron Gates gorge before reaching the Black Sea coast. Rome conquered the region, then known as Dacia, in the early 2nd century AD, a link that shapes national identity to this day. The modern state began with the union of Wallachia and Moldavia in 1859; independence from the Ottoman Empire was recognised in 1878, and Transylvania and other territories joined after the First World War. Communist rule ended abruptly with the revolution of December 1989. Romania joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007. Transylvania retains a sizeable Hungarian minority, along with the fortified churches and towns built by medieval German-speaking Saxon settlers.

facts: Russia spans eleven time zones and borders fourteen countries, both world records.
It is larger than Pluto's surface area, and covers about an eighth of the world's inhabited land.
Lake Baikal in Siberia holds roughly a fifth of all unfrozen fresh water on Earth.
RU.about: The low Ural Mountains divide Russia into a European west, home to most of the population, and the vast expanse of Siberia and the Far East, which makes up roughly three-quarters of the territory. Across the north lie tundra and the world’s largest belt of coniferous forest, the taiga, much of it on permanently frozen ground. Europe’s longest river, the Volga, flows to the Caspian Sea, while great Siberian rivers such as the Ob, Yenisei and Lena drain north into the Arctic Ocean. The state grew from the principality of Moscow, which rose after the period of Mongol rule; Ivan IV was crowned tsar in 1547, and by the 17th century Russian explorers had reached the Pacific. Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 as a new capital. After the 1917 revolution Russia formed the core of the Soviet Union, and the Russian Federation emerged as its successor in 1991. Oil and gas exports dominate the economy.

facts: San Marino claims to be the oldest surviving sovereign state and the oldest republic, traditionally founded in 301.
It is entirely surrounded by Italy and has never had a coastline.
The country has two heads of state, the Captains Regent, who serve six-month terms together.
SM.about: The republic is built around Monte Titano, a limestone ridge in the foothills of the Apennines that rises sharply above the plain, only about ten kilometres from the Adriatic coast at Rimini. Three medieval towers crown its summits, and the walled historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. According to tradition the state was founded by Marinus, a stonemason from the Dalmatian island of Rab who sought refuge on the mountain. Its isolation and steep terrain helped it survive centuries of Italian power struggles, and it remained independent during Italian unification, partly in gratitude for sheltering Garibaldi in 1849; a friendship treaty with Italy followed in 1862. Its governing statutes of 1600 are among the oldest constitutional documents still in force. The territory is divided into nine municipalities called castelli. Tourism, banking, small industry and the sale of collectable stamps and coins have long supported the economy.

facts: Serbia lost its coastline when Montenegro voted for independence in 2006.
Belgrade sits where the Sava meets the Danube and has been destroyed and rebuilt dozens of times.
The country is a major exporter of raspberries, supplying a large share of the world's frozen crop.
RS.about: Northern Serbia is flat and fertile: the province of Vojvodina lies on the Pannonian Plain, crossed by the Danube and the Tisza, and is home to Hungarian and several other minorities. South of the Danube the land becomes hilly and then mountainous, with the Great Morava valley forming a natural corridor that has carried trade and armies between central Europe and the Aegean for centuries. On the Romanian border, the Danube squeezes through the Iron Gates gorge. A powerful medieval Serbian kingdom, ruled by the Nemanjić dynasty, was followed by centuries of Ottoman rule; uprisings beginning in 1804 won autonomy, and full independence was recognised in 1878. Serbia became the core of Yugoslavia after 1918. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia does not recognise. Serbian is written in both Cyrillic and Latin scripts, and the country is a candidate for EU membership, with agriculture and manufacturing important to its economy.

facts: Bratislava is the only national capital that borders two other countries, Austria and Hungary.
Slovakia has one of the highest numbers of castles and châteaux per person in the world.
It became an independent state for the first time in the modern era in 1993, on splitting from Czechia.
SK.about: Most of Slovakia is mountainous, belonging to the Western Carpathians, which reach their most dramatic in the granite peaks of the High Tatras on the Polish border. Limestone areas such as the Slovak Karst and Slovak Paradise are riddled with caves, gorges and waterfalls. The south is lower and warmer, and the Danubian Lowland, including Žitný ostrov, one of Europe’s largest river islands, is prime farmland. For around a thousand years the territory was part of the Kingdom of Hungary, and Bratislava, then known as Pressburg or Pozsony, served as the coronation city of Hungarian kings from the 16th to the 19th century. In 1918 it joined the Czechs in Czechoslovakia, which emerged from communist rule in the Velvet Revolution of 1989. Slovakia joined the EU and NATO in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2009. Car manufacturing dominates industry, and the country produces more cars per person than anywhere else.

facts: More than half of Slovenia is forested, one of the highest shares in Europe.
The word 'karst', used worldwide for limestone cave landscapes, comes from Slovenia's Kras region.
Its coastline on the Adriatic is only about 47 kilometres long.
SI.about: Few countries pack so much variety into such a small area: the Alps, the Dinaric karst, the edge of the Pannonian Plain and the Mediterranean all meet within Slovenia. The Julian Alps in the north-west, protected as Triglav National Park, hold glacial lakes such as Bled and Bohinj, while beneath the limestone of the south-west lie the Postojna and Škocjan caves, the latter a World Heritage Site. The Sava and Drava rivers drain the east towards the Danube. For centuries the Slovene lands were ruled by the Habsburgs as provinces such as Carniola and Styria. After 1918 they became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and later Yugoslavia. Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991 and secured it after a brief ten-day conflict. It was the first former Yugoslav republic to join the EU, in 2004, and adopted the euro in 2007. Its port of Koper serves much of central Europe.

facts: Spain borders Morocco by land at the enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla on the African coast.
Its highest point, Teide, is on Tenerife in the Canary Islands rather than the mainland.
Madrid, at around 650 metres, is the highest capital city in the European Union.
ES.about: At the heart of Spain lies the Meseta Central, a high, dry plateau ringed and crossed by mountain ranges: the Pyrenees in the north-east, the Cantabrian Mountains along the green Atlantic north, and the Sierra Nevada in Andalusia. Most major rivers, including the Douro, Tagus and Guadalquivir, flow west to the Atlantic, while the Ebro drains east into the Mediterranean. Climates range from rainy Galicia to the semi-arid south-east. Roman Hispania was followed by Visigothic rule and, from 711, by Muslim al-Andalus; the Christian reconquest ended with the fall of Granada in 1492, the same year Columbus sailed west, opening the way to a vast American empire. In the 20th century a civil war from 1936 to 1939 led to Franco’s dictatorship, which ended with his death in 1975 and a democratic constitution in 1978. Spain is divided into 17 autonomous communities, and Catalan, Basque and Galician are co-official in their regions.

facts: Sweden has around 267,000 islands, more than any other country, though most are uninhabited.
The right of public access, allmansrätten, lets anyone walk and camp on most land regardless of who owns it.
It has not fought a war since 1814, one of the longest unbroken stretches of peace of any country.
SE.about: Sweden stretches for about 1,500 kilometres from the Baltic south to Lapland, well beyond the Arctic Circle. Mountains run along the Norwegian border, but most of the country is low, forest-covered and dotted with lakes; Vänern is the largest lake in the European Union. The land is still rising after the weight of the ice sheet was removed, most noticeably on the High Coast of the Gulf of Bothnia. Gustav Vasa broke away from the Danish-led Kalmar Union in 1523, and in the 17th century Sweden became a great power ruling much of the Baltic rim, before losing Finland to Russia in 1809. It kept to neutrality through both world wars, joined the EU in 1995 and became a member of NATO in 2024. Forestry and iron ore from mines such as Kiruna underpin a strong engineering and export industry. Most people live in the south, while the north is home to the Sámi.

facts: Switzerland has four official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
It is a direct democracy where citizens vote on referendums several times a year, and it joined the UN only in 2002.
Bern is the seat of government, but the country has no formally designated capital city in its constitution.
CH.about: Switzerland falls into three natural regions: the Alps, which cover about 60 percent of the land; the Jura hills in the north-west; and between them the Swiss Plateau, where most people live and the major cities and farmland are found. The Rhine and Rhône both rise in the Swiss Alps, earning the country its nickname as the water tower of Europe, and large lakes such as Geneva and Constance lie on its borders. The Confederation traces its origin to an alliance of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden in 1291; its independence from the Holy Roman Empire was formally recognised in 1648, and its permanent neutrality in 1815. The modern federal state, made up of 26 cantons, dates from the constitution of 1848. Although surrounded by EU members, Switzerland has stayed outside the Union. Banking, pharmaceuticals, precision engineering and watchmaking drive the economy, and Geneva hosts many international organisations, including the Red Cross.

facts: Ukraine is the largest country lying entirely within Europe, ahead of France and Spain.
Its chernozem black soils are among the most fertile in the world, making it a major grain exporter.
Kyiv is one of the oldest cities in Eastern Europe, a major centre by the 10th century.
UA.about: Most of Ukraine is open plain and steppe, with the Carpathians rising only in the far west and the Crimean Mountains along the southern tip of the Crimean peninsula. The Dnipro, its great river, flows south through the centre, dividing the country into a Right Bank and a Left Bank before reaching the Black Sea; the south also faces the shallow Sea of Azov. After the era of Kyivan Rus’, the Cossack Hetmanate of the 17th century became a formative chapter of national history, but Ukrainian lands were later divided between the Russian and Habsburg empires. A short-lived independent state after 1917 gave way to Soviet rule, which brought the Holodomor famine of 1932–33; the Chornobyl nuclear disaster followed in 1986. Ukraine declared independence in August 1991. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, a move not recognised by most countries, and launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022. Agriculture, steel and heavy industry have long anchored the economy.

facts: The United Kingdom is made up of four countries: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Its only land border is with Ireland, running across the island of Ireland.
It has no single codified constitution, relying instead on statute, convention and case law.
GB.about: The island of Great Britain, together with the north-east of the island of Ireland and several hundred smaller islands such as the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland, makes up the state. A broad divide runs across it: older, harder rocks form the uplands of the north and west, from the Scottish Highlands to Snowdonia, while the south and east are lower and more fertile. The Severn and the Thames are the longest rivers, and the climate is mild and changeable, moderated by the Atlantic. England and Wales were joined in the 16th century, union with Scotland in 1707 created Great Britain, and Ireland was added in 1801; most of Ireland left in 1922. Britain was the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution and built the largest empire in history. Since 1999 Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have had devolved governments. The UK left the European Union in 2020, and most of its people live in England, especially the south-east.

facts: Vatican City is the smallest sovereign state in the world, at about 0.49 square kilometres.
It is an elective absolute monarchy, with the Pope as head of state chosen by the College of Cardinals.
Almost all of its residents are clergy or Swiss Guards, and citizenship is generally tied to holding office rather than birth.
VA.about: Enclosed by walls on the west bank of the Tiber in Rome, the world’s smallest state grew up around the traditional burial place of Saint Peter, over which St Peter’s Basilica now stands, fronted by Bernini’s colonnaded square. For more than a thousand years popes ruled the Papal States across central Italy, until Italian troops took Rome in 1870 and the papacy refused to accept the loss. The dispute was settled only by the Lateran Treaty of 1929, which created the Vatican City State. It is distinct from the Holy See, the governing body of the Catholic Church, which conducts diplomacy with most countries. The state also owns properties outside its walls, including the papal estate at Castel Gandolfo and several major Roman basilicas. Income comes from donations, the Vatican Museums with the Sistine Chapel, and stamps and coins. The entire territory is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
